                    ### Question
                    In the systematic examination of a pregnant woman at term (37 weeks of gestation), beta-hemolytic colonies are isolated from a vaginal smear, which are identified as Streptococcus agalactiae. What assessment would you make of this finding and what would be the most advisable therapeutic attitude to follow? ?

                    ### Options
                    opa. It does not matter because it is part of the commensal microbiota of the vagina.
opb. Birth by caesarean section is recommended.
opc. The search for Streptococcus agalactiae in pregnant women is not indicated.
opd. Immediate antibiotic treatment to the newborn.
ope. Administer intravenous antibiotic prophylaxis during delivery to the pregnant woman.

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The isolation of Streptococcus agalactiae from a vaginal smear in a pregnant woman at term indicates an increased risk of vertical transmission to the newborn, potentially leading to neonatal infection and increased morbidity and mortality. In this case, intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis is advisable to reduce the risk of early-onset neonatal GBS disease. Immediate antibiotic treatment to the newborn may also be necessary if infection occurs. Caesarean section is not the recommended approach solely based on this finding, and routine screening for Streptococcus agalactiae in pregnant women is indicated to prevent neonatal GBS infection.
